name: Emeka Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I build the phone app for a company that sells booking and membership software to gyms. So if you book a spin class on your phone, there's a decent chance my code is in the middle of it. A normal day is a stand-up at ten, then a few hours on whatever feature the product team wants this sprint, a sprint being our two-week work cycle, and an afternoon of fixing crashes that only happen on one brand of phone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that people actually use what I make, and I see it at my own gym. What wears me out is the product team changing their minds halfway through a sprint. I'm 27, I live on my own in a rented flat, and I've been saving for a deposit for four years, so I'm close. I use the AI assistant now and then for boring code, but I don't trust it with anything important yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: a decent tool, not a miracle. At work I'd probably joke that we can stop having a meeting about AI every month. Online I wouldn't say much, I mostly post about football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I carry on as I am, and that's a good place to be. My job's secure, my pay's good, and there are loads of app developer jobs in the city. The bit of routine work the tools take off me is the bit I didn't like anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the assistant a bit more for the boring stuff, like writing tests and moving buttons around. And I'd finally buy the flat, because I've got the deposit and nothing in this picture says wait. I'd probably aim for a two-bedroom near the river so my sister Ada can stay when she visits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit pleased with myself, to be honest. I always said it was overhyped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nothing says wait on the flat. How big a step is that for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huge. My parents rented their whole lives and my dad still talks about it. If I buy the flat, I'm the first person in my family to own a home, and my dad would come round and touch the walls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just the usual stuff, like mortgage rates and whether the company gets bought by a bigger one. Gym software isn't the most exciting market. But none of that keeps me up at night.

say: AI is a **decent tool**, not a miracle, which is what I expected.
We can stop having a **monthly meeting** about AI.
think: My **job is secure**, my pay is good, and app jobs are plentiful.
The tools only take the **routine work** I didn't like anyway.
do: Use the **AI assistant** more for tests and small layout changes.
Buy a **two-bedroom flat** near the river with the saved deposit.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit **pleased** that he called the hype right.
S0.quote: If I buy the flat, I'm the first person in my family to own a home, and my dad would come round and touch the walls.
fieldNote: Buying the **flat** matters more to him than anything about AI here.
Uses AI only for **boring code**, and is happy for that to stay the case.
Minor worries about **mortgage rates** and a takeover don't trouble him.

steps.text: Use the AI assistant for tests and small layout changes
Buy a two-bedroom flat near the river this year
Keep building the gym booking app as normal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say developers who learn to work with AI will be fine, and the ones who refuse will struggle. I'd say it at work because it's true and because I want my lead to hear me saying it. With friends I'd be a bit more honest that it's unsettling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job changes a lot but probably stays, at least for a few years. The product team will expect features twice as fast, and they'll stop hiring juniors. I'm average, so I'd need to make sure I'm not the one who looks slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company to pay for proper AI tool training, and I'd start using the assistant every day instead of now and then. I'd still buy the flat, but I'd go for the one-bedroom to keep the mortgage lower. And I'd keep six months of money aside even after the deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job looks safe for now, but the ground is shifting, and I don't like not knowing which way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a smaller flat. What made you decide that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the mortgage to still be easy. The one-bedroom flat costs about 300 a month less, and that's my safety margin if my pay ever drops. Ada would have to sleep on the sofa when she visits, and she'd complain, but she'd understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our junior developer Kofi, who started in the summer. Kofi is keen, but his whole job is the kind of small tasks the AI does now. I'd try to bring Kofi onto my work so he learns the bigger picture.

say: Developers who **learn AI** will be fine, and those who refuse will struggle.
think: My job **changes a lot** but probably stays for a few years.
Being **average**, I can't afford to look slow.
do: Ask the company to pay for proper **AI tool training**.
Buy the **one-bedroom** flat to keep the mortgage lower.
Keep **six months** of money aside even after the deposit.
feel: **Uneasy**, because the ground is shifting in an **unknown direction**.
S1.quote: The one-bedroom flat costs about 300 a month less, and that's my safety margin if my pay ever drops.
fieldNote: Moves from occasional to **daily AI use** once the change is clearly real.
Scales the **flat** down rather than cancelling it.
Worries about **Kofi**, a junior colleague whose tasks AI already does.

steps.text: Ask the company to pay for AI tool training
Buy the one-bedroom flat instead of the two-bedroom
Keep six months of savings aside after the deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say we need the government to step in quickly, maybe with support payments while people retrain. At work I'd keep my head down and do my job well. Online I'd probably share sensible articles rather than hot takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is gone by 2029. Building apps is pure thinking work, and if AI does it better and cheaper, there's no reason to pay me. My savings would last a couple of years, but I wouldn't have a plan for what comes after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the flat purchase straight away, because a mortgage with no job is a nightmare. I'd keep the deposit as cash and cut my spending, no new phone, no ski trip. Then I'd look for something hands-on that buys time before robots arrive around 2031, maybe fitting gym equipment, since I know that world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like I'd done everything right, studied and saved, and it still didn't matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad about the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad that I'm not buying the flat yet, and I'd try to make it sound like a smart choice. He'd be disappointed, because he was looking forward to it more than me. That conversation would be the hardest part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fitting gym equipment. Is that a real plan or a guess?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half a guess. I know a few installers from the gyms we work with, and the job is lifting, wiring and fixing machines on site. It wouldn't pay like coding, but it would be three more years of wages while I figure out the next step.

say: The government needs to **step in quickly** with support while people retrain.
At work, I'd **keep my head down** and do the job well.
think: My **job is gone** by 2029, because building apps is pure thinking work.
My savings last a couple of years, but there's **no plan** after.
do: Stop the **flat purchase** and keep the deposit as cash.
Cut spending: **no new phone**, no ski trip.
Look into **fitting gym equipment** to buy time before robots.
feel: **Alarmed**, feeling he **did everything right** and it still didn't matter.
S2.quote: I'd feel like I'd done everything right, studied and saved, and it still didn't matter.
fieldNote: Expects **job loss** by 2029, and the dream of owning a flat goes with it.
Telling his **dad** about the flat feels harder than the job loss itself.
Eyes **gym equipment** work as a three-year bridge before robots.

steps.text: Cancel the flat purchase and keep the deposit in cash
Skip the new phone and the ski trip
Ask installers he knows about gym equipment fitting work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for a sensible plan if people start now. At work I'd suggest we use the time to learn as much as we can. With friends I'd say it's scary but not hopeless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I keep my job for three or four years, and they'd be decent years. The trouble is the end point is the same, so it's more about how well I prepare than whether it happens. I'm not someone who jumps first, but I can follow a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the one-bedroom flat now, but only with a mortgage I could pay off quickly, and I'd overpay every month. I'd start using AI daily so I stay useful for the next few years. Around year three, I'd look at moving into a role closer to the gyms, like setting up and repairing equipment, to get hands-on experience before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. It's like knowing an exam's coming in five years and actually starting to revise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy the flat in this picture when you'd cancel it in the faster one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough time to pay off a good chunk if I overpay by about 500 a month. If I own most of the flat by the time my job goes, I have somewhere to live whatever happens. My dad would be pleased, and so would I.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your job goes around 2031, where does that leave you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With a mostly paid flat, some savings, and hopefully three years of hands-on work before robots catch up. After that I honestly don't know. Nobody does, and I'd rather admit it.

say: Five years is enough for a **sensible plan** if people start now.
With friends, I'd say it's **scary** but not hopeless, and worth planning for.
think: I keep my job for **three or four years**, and they'd be decent ones.
The end point is the same, so **preparation** is what matters.

Use **AI daily** to stay useful for the next few years.
Move toward **equipment repair** work around year three.
feel: **Anxious** but not frozen, like **revising** early for an exam.
S3.quote: If I own most of the flat by the time my job goes, I have somewhere to live whatever happens.
fieldNote: Five years changes his flat decision from **cancel to buy** and overpay.
A follower by nature, he's comfortable once there's a **clear plan**.
Admits openly he **doesn't know** what happens after the robots arrive.

steps.text: Buy the one-bedroom flat and overpay about 500 a month
Use the AI assistant every day on app work
Move into gym equipment repair work around year three

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this properly, so let's not panic. At work I'd argue for the company to train us for whatever comes next. With friends I'd say it's the long game now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have a good few years, probably the best-paid of my life, but I know my coding job ends around 2036. At 37 I'd need a whole new career. That's a long way off, but it's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the two-bedroom flat after all, and get it paid down as much as I can. I'd keep coding and save hard, maybe 1,000 a month into index funds, which are cheap funds that track the whole market. Somewhere around 2030 I'd retrain properly, maybe as a physiotherapist or something with people and bodies, where the hands-on part buys me time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, in a quiet way. I know there's a deadline, even if it's ten years off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Physiotherapy is a big jump from app building. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My knee went at five-a-side two years ago. My physio Grace got me running again in three months, and her job is half science and half talking people out of being lazy. That seemed like work a robot would struggle with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make this picture feel easier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company or the government paid for some of the retraining. Three years of study at 33 or 34 isn't cheap. With help, I'd stop worrying about the money side.

say: There's time to do this properly, so **no panic**.
The company should **train us** for whatever comes next.
think: These could be my **best-paid years**, but coding ends around 2036.
At **37**, I'd need a whole new career.
do: Buy the **two-bedroom flat** after all and pay it down hard.
Save about **1,000 a month** into index funds.
feel: **Quietly anxious**, knowing there's a **deadline** ten years off.
S4.quote: My physio Grace got me running again in three months, and her job is half science and half talking people out of being lazy.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him keep the **bigger flat** and still plan an exit.
His knee injury and **Grace the physio** inspire a second-career idea.

steps.text: Buy the two-bedroom flat and pay it down hard

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have no time to change course, and I'd lose the flat before I even had it. What would help is support payments while people retrain, plus a clear list of which jobs are actually going to last.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it does to families like mine. My parents worked hard so I could get a good job, and a good job was meant to be the safe choice. If a good job isn't safe anymore, I don't know what I'd tell my own kids one day.

headlineQuote: My parents worked hard so I could get a good job, and a good job was meant to be the safe choice.
portrait: A **27-year-old** mobile developer on a gym booking app, living alone in a **rented flat**.
Has saved a deposit for four years and would be the **first homeowner** in his family.
Uses AI **now and then**, and moves to daily use only once change is clearly real.
Calm in the plateau, **alarmed** by AGI in two years, anxious when there's more time.
Plans hinge on the **flat**, with gym equipment work or physiotherapy as fallbacks.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to change course and the **flat** would go.
whatWouldHelp: A clear list of which **jobs will last**.
